text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- Germany's state secretary in the Interior Ministry Karl Schelter expects Germany to keep up its border control to Austria until the year 2000, even though Austria will become a member of the European Union's Schengen agreement by the end of this year.
- Experts are discussing raising the minimum age for early retirement.

- The conservative People's Party says the social plan for the privatisation of Austria's postal service Post & Telekom Austria will have to be renegotiated, as sending employees to early retirement is against the government's plans to reform the pension system.
- Chipmaker AMS will invest one billion schillings in a new production facility.
- Jam maker Darbo will pay out a dividend of 18 schillings for 1996 after none last year, as exports jumped 74 percent to 167 million schillings.
- German electricity giant Bayernwerk is pushing hard into the Austrian energy market.
- Lauda Air posted a loss of 142.9 million schillings in its half-year pretax, although it narrowed from the 165.6 million schilling loss posted in the year-ago period.
- Billion-schilling orders from Poland and Germany could be an important step for builder Rogner to stabilise his loss-making company.
- The Vienna stock exchange will not take legal action against Bank Austria saying it had not breached the shareholder's law.
- Fibremaker Lenzing hopes to restructure its lossmaking U.S. subsidiary for the last time as over-capacities and falling prices increase losses.
- Austrians are the least sick since 1956 as the government has installed stricter control and higher fees.
- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger says the plan to cut funding of the premiums of building societies was negotiated with the conservative junior coalition partner.
